data.generator_code:
def generate(rng, n):
    if n <= 1:
        return [[rng.randint(-10**9, 10**9)]]
    has_dup = rng.choice([True, False])
    base = rng.randint(-10**8, 10**8)
    if has_dup:
        nums = [base + i for i in range(n - 1)]
        nums.append(nums[rng.randint(0, n - 2)])
        rng.shuffle(nums)
        return [nums]
    else:
        nums = [base + i for i in range(n)]
        rng.shuffle(nums)
        return [nums]

def generate_worst(rng, n):
    base = rng.randint(-10**8, 10**8)
    nums = [base + i for i in range(n)]
    return [nums]

data.key_insight: A hash set stores unique elements. If the number of unique elements in `nums` is less than the total length of `nums`, then at least one element must appear more than once.

steps.title: Convert to Set
steps.detail: Pass the list `nums` into Python's `set()` constructor to remove all duplicate values, leaving only distinct elements.

steps.title: Compare Lengths
steps.detail: Compare the size of the set with the length of the original `nums` list.

steps.title: Return Result
steps.detail: If the length of the set is strictly less than `len(nums)`, return `True` (duplicates exist). Otherwise, return `False`.

data.overview: The algorithm determines if an array contains any duplicate values by converting it into a hash set. Since a hash set only stores unique elements, comparing its size to the original list length instantly reveals if duplicates were removed.
data.intuition: Imagine checking guest IDs at a club entrance by tossing them into a drop box. If you put all the IDs into a distinct box and the box has fewer slips than the total number of guests, someone snuck in twice.

flow_nodes.detail: Lengths are equal, meaning all elements are distinct.

pitfalls: Using a nested loop approach which leads to O(n^2) time limit exceeded on large arrays.

data.pattern_summary: A Hash set allows O(1) time complexity lookups. Reach for it when you need to quickly check if an item has been seen before.

pattern_options.name: Hash set
pattern_options.feedback: Correct. Storing elements in a hash set lets us check for duplicates in constant time on average.

pattern_options.name: Two pointers
pattern_options.feedback: Incorrect. Two pointers usually apply to sorted arrays or searching for pairs meeting a condition, but order does not matter here.

pattern_options.name: Sliding window
pattern_options.feedback: Incorrect. Sliding window is used for contiguous subarrays of a specific size or condition, not checking all elements for duplicates.

pattern_options.name: Binary search
pattern_options.feedback: Incorrect. Binary search requires sorted data and a specific target, which does not fit finding any arbitrary duplicate.

signals.phrase: any value appears at least twice
signals.hint: Implies we are tracking the existence of elements we have already encountered.
Suggests we want to know if all items are unique.

data.brute_force_idea: Compare every element in the array against every other element using nested loops to check for a match.
data.brute_force_why: The outer loop runs n times and the inner loop runs n times for each outer iteration, resulting in n squared comparisons.
data.bottleneck: Line 4 repeatedly scans previous elements for every new element, causing redundant checks that slow down execution.
bottleneck_hints: Look at how many times we inspect the same values.
Think about what information you could store as you iterate so you do not need a second loop.
Consider a data structure that can remember what you have already seen in O(1) time.

events.label: Coach: why the complexity is what it is

data.insight: The brute-force approach compares every pair of elements, resulting in quadratic time complexity. The optimized approach leverages a hash set to identify duplicates. Because a hash set only stores unique elements, comparing the length of the set to the length of the original list immediately reveals if any duplicates were filtered out.

derivation.note: Converting the list to a set requires iterating through all n elements and inserting them into the hash table.

data.time_summary: While the step counter shows exactly 1 step for line 3 because it is a single Python expression, the underlying C-level set construction must process all n elements. This yields a theoretical time complexity of O(n). The measured wall-clock growth of n^1.31 reflects practical overheads like memory allocation and hash collision resolution on the tested input sizes.
data.space_summary: The space complexity is O(n) because the set stores up to n unique elements in memory.
data.takeaway: To find duplicates or track elements you have already seen, trade O(n) space for O(1) lookup time by using a hash set.
mistakes: Converting the entire list to a set prevents early-exit optimization, forcing the algorithm to process all elements even if a duplicate exists at the very beginning.
Forgetting that hash collisions can degrade set insertion and lookup times from O(1) to O(n) in the worst case.
